items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: How I keep a multiplayer browser city alive with zero players online
items.summary: I'm a solo dev from Uruguay building Balak City, a multiplayer open-world city that runs in the browser: one shared city where everyone walks, drives, runs missions and buys businesses at the same time. It's plain JavaScript and Canvas 2D, no engine. The question that shaped the whole architecture was simple: what happens to the city when nobody is online? In a lot of browser multiplayer games, the first player to join a room becomes the "host" and simulates the world for everyone. That works until: the host is on a cheap phone and the whole city stutters for everyone, the host switches tabs and the browser throttles their timers, the host leaves and the world freezes or resets. For a city that's supposed to feel alive (traffic, pedestrians, police, factories producing goods), none of that was acceptable. The city is simulated by a headless copy of the game itself, running on a small VPS: The game client is a single HTML page. The server runs that same page in a headless browser with a special key in the URL that tells it "you are the host". items.title: Supabase email sign-in and a profiles table for iOS, done safely
items.summary: Almost every iOS app I start needs the same first hour of work: email sign-in, a place to keep per-user data, and a way to make sure users can only touch their own rows. This post walks through the setup I use: the SQL, the Swift, and the three mistakes to avoid. It assumes you know basic SwiftUI and have a free Supabase project. Supabase Auth stores credentials in auth.users. You don't add your own columns there. Instead you create a public.profiles table whose primary key is the auth user's id: create table if not exists public.profiles ( id uuid primary key references auth.users (id) on delete cascade, email text, full_name text, avatar_url text, created_at timestamptz not null default now(), updated_at timestamptz not null default now() ); on delete cascade matters: when the auth user is deleted, the profile goes with it. No orphans. The key in your app is public. Anyone can extract it. So the key is not your security. items.summary: A lower monthly price can hide an upfront fee or a longer commitment. A comparison tool should show its assumptions before ranking offers. For a fixed evaluation period, keep the upfront cost, monthly charge, number of months and unconditional credits separate. Do not subtract a conditional rebate until its conditions are met. function totalCost({ upfront, monthly, months, credits = 0 }) { const values = [upfront, monthly, months, credits]; if (!values.every(Number.isFinite)) throw new Error("Use finite numbers"); if (values.some(v => v < 0)) throw new Error("Use non-negative inputs"); if (!Number.isInteger(months)) throw new Error("Use whole months"); return upfront + monthly * months - credits; } Offer A: zero upfront plus $85 per month for 24 months = $2,040. Offer B: $600 upfront plus $40 per month for 24 months = $1,560. The difference is $480 before taxes, fees or financing. These are illustrative numbers, not current carrier offers. Zero months should return upfront minus credits. Zero upfront cost is valid. Negative values, infinity and missing numbers should be rejected. items.title: Node.js Share Card Cache: 3 Contracts for Replaceable Open Graph Images
items.summary: A media catalog that removes backgrounds from product photos should cache Open Graph share card images independently of the cutout operation. Producing a better cutout and delivering a preview repeatedly have different lifetimes. Reprocessing the original on every crawler request makes bandwidth depend on preview traffic, even when the title and image have not changed. Short answer: generate an Open Graph card once per content version, cache it under a key derived from the title and template, and regenerate when those inputs change. For product photos, include the source image revision and background-removal settings in that version too; otherwise a better cutout can remain hidden behind an unchanged title. Keep the processing contract, object identity, and delivery reference separate so replacing an API does not require rewriting the catalog. Start with bytes. A crawler requesting an existing preview doesn't need a new background-removal operation, and a title edit doesn't inherently require another pass over the product photograph. items.title: Why a soft shadow prints as white dots: checking customer images before UV printing
items.summary: At Kloniko customers upload their own images to print on a figure: a face, a logo on a torso, a pattern on the legs. In the configurator the image looks right. Sometimes the printed part did not: stubble, soft shadows and blush came out as whitish specks. The image was fine. The preview was wrong. A UV printer does not blend ink with the surface. To make colours show on a coloured part, it first lays down a white underbase wherever the image has any pixel, and then prints the colour on top. The underbase has no "30% opacity". A pixel with alpha 60 out of 255 gets 100% white under it and only a little colour over it. On screen, the browser blends that pixel with the skin-coloured part, and you see a soft shadow. On the part, you get an almost white dot. So we render two versions of every uploaded image in the browser, on a canvas: // what the screen shows: normal alpha blending with the part colour screen = src * a + part * (1 - a) // what the printer makes: colour over a white base, wherever a > 0 uv = src * a + white * (1 - a) If the two differ a lot over a noticeable area, the customer has a problem they cannot see. Our test for it is simple: a grid of semi-transparent brown dots

items.title: 5,100 draw calls to 270: 3D building instructions for a 1,689-part brick model on a phone
items.summary: We build BrickPlay: step-by-step 3D building instructions that open in the browser from a QR code on the box. No app, the builder just scans and builds on a phone. Small models were fine. Then we loaded a 1,689-part model, and on phones the step animation stuttered badly. Here is what was wrong and how we fixed it with three.js. We load models with LDrawLoader. Every LDraw part becomes three objects: a mesh, its edges, and the "conditional" lines that draw the outline of curved surfaces. That is three draw calls per part, plus the shadow pass. For 1,689 parts this gave about 5,100 draw calls and 28–31 ms of CPU per frame on a strong desktop. On a phone it was several times worse. On desktop we already avoided this by baking: everything that is already built is merged into one buffer per colour, in world coordinates. The parts are sorted by step, so "show steps 1…N" is just a draw range. No scene rebuild, about 100 draw calls, 3.5 ms per frame. The catch is memory. Baking copies the geometry of every part. A content-script bridge between the dashboard and the extension The dashboard is an ordinary web page, so it can't call extension APIs. items.summary: Property management teams should choose browser-upload storage by its trust boundary and retention controls, not by whether its SDK can mint a presigned URL. For training artifacts, the browser should receive permission for one object, for a short window, with a server-owned key and a separately enforced retention policy. The storage provider matters after those rules are clear. A useful design has three planes: a Node.js service authorizes an upload, the browser sends bytes directly to object storage, and a worker records completion and applies retention metadata. That separation keeps credentials out of the browser, but it does not make the browser trustworthy. It can still retry, abandon a multipart upload, or send an unexpected content type. I treat those as normal states, not exceptional ones. Ownership decides the boundary. No exceptions. A presigned URL is a bearer capability. Anyone who obtains it can use it until it expires or its constraints stop matching the request. The API should therefore decide the archive identity before it signs anything: property, course, employee or cohort, artifact type, maximum size, and an immutable object key. items.title: Webhook Retry Queue: Delayed Jobs and Idempotency in Node.js
items.summary: Short answer: treat a webhook retry queue as an at-least-once transport, and make the durable business change idempotent with a stable event identity and a database transaction. The deciding constraint is the gap between doing work and acknowledging it. A worker can commit a change, lose its process before the acknowledgement is recorded, and receive the same job again. No reasonable retry policy can infer whether that first change happened. Delayed jobs help recovery; they do not close that gap. For an AI application, that distinction matters twice. A repeated state change can corrupt customer state, while a repeated call to a model or external API can consume latency and usage budget without producing a new result. Keep the queue simple, but make its boundaries explicit. There are usually two independent retry loops. The webhook sender retries when it does not receive a timely success response. The receiving system may then retry its queued work after a timeout, a process restart, or an unavailable dependency. items.summary: Short answer: start with a free uptime monitor for the public health path, but do not confuse a green check with an explanation of an incident. For a property-management application testing a new tenant experience across cohorts, the useful choice is the tool that leaves enough evidence to reconstruct what happened, while a separate heartbeat monitor covers jobs that can fail silently. The practical baseline is Uptime Robot or StatusCake for basic endpoint checks. Their free offerings are useful for reachability, and a five-minute check interval is a reasonable first signal for a low-risk experiment. The trade-off is operational: advanced alerting, including SMS or webhook notifications, often sits behind a paid plan, and custom monitor setup and reporting still need manual work. Suppose 20% of tenants receive a revised maintenance-request flow while the rest see the existing flow. At 09:10, the application health endpoint is green. items.title: Props Drilling in React
items.summary: When building React applications, we use props to pass data from one component to another. But what happens when we need to pass data through multiple components, even when some of those components don't need that data? This is called Props Drilling. Let's understand it with a simple example. Props Drilling happens when we pass data from a parent component to a deeply nested child component through multiple intermediate components. In simple words, we pass props through components just to reach another component that actually needs the data. Imagine we have three components: App Profile User The App component has a username, and the User component needs to display it. But the User component is inside the Profile component. Let's see how we pass the data. App.jsx function App() { const username = "Lokesh"; return ; } export default App; Here, App sends the username to Profile. Profile.jsx function Profile({ username }) { return ; } Profile receives the username and passes it to User. User.jsx function User({ username }) { return Welcome, {username} ; } export default User; User finally receives the username and displays it. Output: Welcome, Lokesh Look at how the data travels: App |

items.title: Flisk: run a multi-service app on your laptop with one command (and what it does not do)
items.summary: Flisk is an open-source command-line tool that runs every part of a multi-service app (API, website, worker, database) on your own computer with one command. The README says a small app starts "as two local processes in about a second", with no Docker. Repo URL: https://github.com/flisk-sh/flisk Language: TypeScript CLI (Ink terminal UI). Runs on Node.js 22.12+. Your own services can be Node, Python, Go, Rust, JVM, Ruby or PHP. Try it: npx @flisk-sh/flisk demo. No signup, no global install. With Docker and Tilt it starts a six-service restaurant demo with Postgres, one gateway and live reload. Without them it starts a small menu app as two local processes and prints their URLs (usually http://localhost:3000; it picks a free port if that one is busy), and flisk down stops it. CLI: flisk create asks a few questions and writes a project that runs. flisk import . reads a docker-compose.yml and writes one service.json per Compose service, keeping ports, names and env values. flisk up starts services in health-checked dependsOn order and prints a *.localhost URL for each. flisk status, flisk logs and flisk doctor show what is running and what is wrong. flisk down stops everything. items.summary: I was building the coin system for Eyerone, a social platform with live streaming and virtual gifts: users buy a coin pack through Stripe Checkout, Stripe calls my webhook, and my server credits the coins. It worked perfectly in testing. Then I noticed something in the database: some users had been credited twice for a single payment. No hacking, no bugs in Stripe. Just a classic race condition in my own code. Here's what happened and the fix. This is roughly what my fulfillment logic looked like: async function fulfillOrder(sessionId) { const order = await Order.findOne({ stripeSessionId: sessionId }); if (order.status === 'paid') return; // already handled ✅ ...right? order.status = 'paid'; await order.save(); await User.updateOne( { _id: order.userId }, { $inc: { coins: order.coins } } ); } Looks safe. We check the status before doing anything. So how did coins get credited twice? Two things are true in production: Stripe can deliver the same event more than once. items.title: Implement Multer in Node.js for User Profile Picture Uploads: 4 Storage Boundaries
items.summary: Short answer: use Multer as the multipart boundary, not as the storage policy. Validate the upload on the server, derive the object key from authenticated tenant data, write to private object storage, and return an application reference. For an e-commerce system retaining signed order documents until an explicit deletion deadline, the same rule matters more than the image format: storage must not become an accidental authorization layer. The practical design is a small upload handler plus an application-owned object-storage adapter. It works for a user avatar, but its important test case is a signed document that must stay isolated from every other tenant and disappear on schedule. Multer parses multipart/form-data and can enforce a byte limit before the handler processes the file. It does not know which tenant the caller belongs to. It does not make a browser-provided key trustworthy. Those checks stay in the application. I would keep three identifiers in the storage key: tenant, business object, and an opaque object ID. items.title: Your cron job will fire twice. Design for it.
items.summary: Every tutorial for scheduled work has the same shape. A cron expression, a route handler, a loop over users, a call to an email API. It runs on the author's machine for two days and then it ships. Then production happens. The platform retries a 502 that actually succeeded. A deploy lands mid-run and two workers process the same batch. The retry after a rate limit sends the digest a second time. A customer forwards the duplicate to support, and someone writes a ticket titled "we got this twice," and that is the first time anybody thinks about delivery semantics. Cron is a trigger, not a scheduler. The moment your work leaves the process, you are in at-least-once territory, and at-least-once means duplicates are not an edge case. They are the contract. The fix is not a sent_at column you check before sending, because check-then-send has a race and you will find it at 3 a.m. with two workers that both read null. items.title: The Future of Micro-Frontends: How to Combine Module Federation with Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
items.summary: Client-side Module Federation has a well-known weakness, the browser downloads a shell, then fetches remotes, then renders. Users stare at a blank page, and crawlers may see very little. For content-heavy or SEO-sensitive products, that's a deal-breaker, and it's why teams keep asking the same question, can we get independently deployed micro-frontends **and* server-rendered HTML?* The answer is yes, with caveats. Module Federation supports server-side rendering, and the same model that works in the browser transfers to Node, a host fetches code from remotes at runtime and renders it on the server. But SSR raises the stakes. You now have two runtimes to keep consistent, a network dependency inside your render path, and a security boundary you didn't have before. This guide explains how the pieces fit, shows a working configuration pattern, and is candid about where the ecosystem is solid and where it isn't. In client-only federation, a remote publishes a remoteEntry.js, and the browser loads it on demand. With SSR, each application builds twice, a browser bundle and a server bundle, each with its own federation entry. Request ──► Host server (Node) │ 1. fetch remote's SERVER entry

items.title: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect: Why the Tooltip Flashes, Then Jumps
items.summary: Picture a tooltip that should sit above a button. For one frame it shows up at the top of the box, then it jumps into place. The measurement was right. It ran too late. useEffect let the browser paint the first, wrong position. React updates the DOM, then the browser paints what the user sees. There is a gap between those two, like the moment before a curtain opens. useLayoutEffect runs in that gap, while the curtain is closed. useEffect runs after the curtain opens, once the user can already see the frame. Both take the same arguments: a setup function, a dependency list, and an optional cleanup. The only difference is when the setup runs. One update, from commit to paint 1. React writes the DOM — The new elements are in the document 2. useLayoutEffect — Measure and correct, still invisible 3. Browser paints — This is the frame the user sees 4. useEffect — Fetch, subscribe, log The user only sees the frame after useLayoutEffect has finished. useEffect is the one for work that talks to the outside world: a fetch, a subscription, a timer, a log line. items.title: Rust Leaves Top 10 in TIOBE Index, Making Room for Go
items.summary: "In November's edition of the TIOBE Index, Rust has dropped out of Top 10," writes I-Programmer, noting that Rust ceded the #10 position to Go. "At the same time, another Google-originated language, Dart, has entered the top 20 ousting Julia after only one month." TIOBE explains Dart's popularity is mainly being driven by Flutter, Google's framework for building cross-platform mobile applications. In fact, Flutter has become one of the major technologies for cross-platform mobile app development. The Dart language itself is not particularly unique, although it incorporates many modern programming language features. Its success is largely driven by the strength of the Flutter ecosystem and the convenience of developing applications for multiple platforms using a single codebase... [In November's ranking] Visual Basic has also lost two places, making room for R and SQL in the Top 10. Further down the ranking, Assembly has re-entered the Top 20. So TIOBE ranks the top 10 languages in November as Python, C, Java, C++, C#, JavaScript, R, SQL, Visual Basic, and Go. items.summary: A small .NET service can look healthy in a quiet test. Then it can fail on a busy morning because it opens a new network client for every call. The failure is often a shortage of TCP ports, not a bug in the ERP API it is calling. Some quick terms first. HttpClient is the .NET class that sends HTTP requests and reads the replies. HTTP is the protocol used by most web and REST APIs. A connection pool is a set of open network connections that a client can reuse. TCP is the transport that carries those connections. After a connection closes, the operating system keeps its port in a short "TIME-WAIT" state, so the port cannot be used again at once. Domain Name System, or DNS, is the directory that maps a name such as api.example.com to a network address. This write-up is from Aimpex Resources Group LLC. items.summary: This post was originally published in Portuguese on my blog: .NET 8 e .NET 9 saíram de suporte no dia do maior Patch Tuesday da história. On Tuesday, November 10, two things happened that look like separate news items and that, in my opinion, are the same story. .NET 8 and .NET 9 went out of support. And on the same day Microsoft shipped the largest Patch Tuesday I've ever seen: close to 1,100 security fixes, depending on who is counting. The schedule had been announced since June. On November 10, 2026, .NET 8 (LTS) and .NET 9 (STS) stopped receiving security fixes and technical support. .NET 9 ended together with 8 because the support window for STS releases was stretched from 18 to 24 months, and the math landed on the same date. The official recommendation is to move to .NET 10, which is LTS and supported until November 2028. Your application keeps running, nobody is going to switch anything off, but whatever gets discovered from now on won't be fixed for those versions. items.title: Gate features at compile time: a Roslyn source generator for Keyright entitlements
items.summary: Entitlement checks have a way of multiplying. One feature needs export.pdf, another needs reports.scheduled, a third needs a seats limit — and each one grows its own little block of "resolve the license, read the entitlement, decide what to do on failure." Copy that block around a codebase and it drifts: one call site throws, another returns false, a third forgets to check at all, and somewhere a string literal says exprot.pdf and silently denies a feature to every paying customer. The checks are individually trivial and collectively a liability. This is exactly the kind of repetitive, error-prone, mechanical code a Roslyn source generator exists to remove. Instead of writing the guard, you declare the gate with an attribute and let the generator emit a correct, uniform guard at compile time — and, because the generator sees your whole compilation, it can validate every entitlement name against your declared catalog and fail the build on a typo. This post builds that generator against the Keyright SDK. items.title: Segurança em aplicações .NET na era da IA: o prompt que eu uso para revisar código
items.summary: Peça para um assistente de IA: "crie um endpoint que retorna o pedido pelo id". Em segundos você tem um código limpo, compilando e funcionando. E, na maioria das vezes, com uma falha clássica: qualquer usuário logado consegue ler o pedido de qualquer outro usuário, só trocando o número na URL. A IA não errou. Ela fez exatamente o que foi pedido: algo que funciona. Segurança raramente está no pedido, e o modelo otimiza para o caminho feliz. O problema é que hoje se escreve muito mais código, muito mais rápido, e se lê bem menos do que se escreve. É o que eu repito para os clientes da Dotcode: IA amplifica o processo que já existe. Se o seu processo de desenvolvimento não tem segurança, a IA não resolve isso. Ela escala a vulnerabilidade na mesma velocidade em que escala a entrega. items.title: Building a read-aloud screen: phrases, tappable words and a finger that drifts
items.summary: Background A lot of what I read is still on paper: letters from the bank, school handouts, a recipe, a library book. I often want to listen to them instead, and I want to follow the words while I listen, so my eyes have something to hold on to. So I built Outloud Reader. You take a photo of a printed page (or open a PDF, or paste text), the app reads it out loud, and the phrase being spoken is highlighted on screen. It runs on iOS and Android, and it can translate a page before reading it. This post is about the reading screen, the part people look at for minutes at a time. It turned out to be the hardest screen in the app to get right. What I wanted from it: the current phrase highlighted, the current sentence easy to find, the rest of the page calm; tap any word to jump the audio there; a "just listen" mode with the text hidden, which you can still peek at; Japanese, Chinese and Thai behaving like any other language. Word-by-word highlighting, like karaoke. It is still in the code as an option, but it was exhausting to watch. items.title: I built a liquid-glass Spotify mini player for Windows
items.summary: I wanted a Spotify controller on my desktop that I'd actually enjoy looking at. Not another flat grey box, but something closer to Apple's liquid glass: clear, soft, a little bit alive. So I built one for Windows. Glass Player is a small widget that floats on your desktop, shows what's playing, and gives you play/pause, previous/next, shuffle, seek and "always on top". It appears when Spotify opens and leaves when Spotify closes. It's written in C# with WPF on .NET 8, and it's open source. / glass-player Glass Player A liquid-glass mini player for Spotify on Windows. Late-night vinyl, under glass: a tiny desktop widget that takes its colour from whatever you're listening to. Highlights Real frosted glass. The widget blurs whatever sits behind it with its own blur engine: clean 30 px corners, a thick bright rim, a soft lens ring and a faint pink/cyan refraction fringe. The cover sets the mood. One accent colour is pulled from each album cover and carried through the play button, progress line, glow and dots. Every song re-themes the card. A record that plays. A vinyl disc (the cover is its label) slides out of the sleeve and spins while music plays, and tucks back in when you pause.

items.title: I built a free Mac dictation app that never sends your voice to a server
items.summary: A few months ago my wrists started aching by mid-afternoon. I type for a living, most days for nine to twelve hours, and by evening I was closing the laptop instead of answering one more email. I tried the voice to text apps people recommend. A couple of them are good. Every one I tried wanted a monthly subscription and sent my voice to a server before the text came back, and I've written enough software to know that audio can sit on somebody else's disk for as long as they like. So I built my own, over a few weekends that turned into a few months. I wanted to see whether small open models could do the whole job on a laptop people already own. The result is Purr, a free, open-source menu bar app for macOS. You hold Right Option, talk and let go, and the words get typed into whatever text field has focus. It doesn't need an account, and nothing it hears leaves your Mac. Once the models have downloaded, it works offline. What it does Dictation is the main thing. items.summary: NSCollectionView 有 4 種排版： 排版 1：1 個 Cell（1） 排版 2：2 個 Cell（2） 排版 3：3 個 Cell（1 + 2） 排版 4：5 個 Cell（2 + 3） 畫面目前有 5 個 Cell，使用排版 4（2 + 3） 使用者點擊第一排右側的 Close Button Cell 被刪除，排版依剩餘 Cell 數量重新切換 使用者立即點擊原本的位置 該位置明明有 Close Button，卻沒有觸發刪除 停頓一小段時間後，又可以正常點擊 使用 deleteItems(at:) 刪除 Cell，沒有呼叫 reloadData 只有排版改變時，才會發生點擊後沒有刪除的情況 把 deleteItems(at:) 改成每次都 reloadData，反而每次刪除後都會發生 prepareForReuse 沒有遺漏重置資料 刪除 Cell 時，main thread 上沒有耗時的工作 多次嘗試沒有結果後，改從滑鼠事件本身調查。我請 AI 加入更完整的 Debug Log，觀察： mouseDown 事件實際由哪個 Button 接收 mouseUp 事件的流向 NSEvent.clickCount 的變化 滑鼠目前位置透過 Hit Test 找到的 View 把過濾後的 Log 貼給 AI，能快速分析出情況，節省時間。 快速連續點擊時，Log 出現了一個很特別的現象：clickCount 持續增加，但接收 mouseDown 的 Button 始終是同一個實例。 Click 1 clickCount = 1 mouseDown self = 0xbb545ed00 (Button A) hitTest = Button A Click 2 clickCount = 2 mouseDown self = 0xbb545ed00 (Button A) hitTest = Button B Click 3 clickCount = 3 mouseDown self = 0xbb545ed00 (Button A) hitTest = Button B 這代表： 第一下點擊時，接收事件的是 Button A。 Cell 刪除並重新排版後，滑鼠下方已經變成 Button B（Hit Test 的結果）。 但後續點擊的 mouseDown，仍然由 Button A 接收。 畫面上滑鼠下方的 Button，和實際收到滑鼠事件的 Button，並不是同一個。 TODO（發文前請確認）：目前只觀察到現象，尚未確認 AppKit 為何在連續點擊時沿用舊的接收者，也沒驗證「停頓後恢復」是否與系統雙擊間隔有關。若有實測或文件佐證，請補在這裡；沒有的話，這段維持「觀察到的現象」即可。 在 Button 的 mouseDown 中判斷事件是否真的落在自己身上

items.summary: As developers and researchers, our desktop screens display our most sensitive intellectual property: uncommitted proprietary code, confidential game crash logs, private API keys, and draft academic papers. Yet, many popular desktop translation utilities take an alarming architectural shortcut: they capture your screen and ship the entire raw PNG/JPEG image directly to cloud-hosted computer vision APIs. In this technical breakdown, we explore how to build a Privacy-First Desktop OCR & Translation Architecture on macOS. By leveraging Apple's native Vision Framework and ScreenCaptureKit, we ensure that image frames never leave the user's local machine, while only sanitized textual tokens cross the network boundary. items.title: Bitcoin Plummets 24% in 46 Days as Crypto Falls on Rising Inflation
items.summary: October 3: $84,680 Today: $64,108 Bitcoin dropped 24.2% in 46 days. And it "fell more than 4% on Friday to $68,500," reports Fortune, "wiping out gains built over the past three months and casting doubt on whether its bear market was ever really over." The asset also faces weaker investor appetite, according to crypto analytics provider CryptoQuant. The firm's demand indicator recorded its weakest reading since December 2023, while Bitcoin exchange-traded funds became net sellers again. items.title: I shipped a VPN app on iOS, Mac, Android and Windows without writing a VPN protocol
items.summary: I build mobile apps for a living, mostly on iOS. This year I shipped a VPN called Privalune on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Android and Windows. I did it alone, and the only reason that was possible is one decision I made early: I would not write or bundle a VPN protocol. Every platform I target already ships an IKEv2 client. So the apps are remote controls. They hand the operating system a server and a login, and the OS runs the tunnel. This post covers how that works on each platform, what the backend looks like, and where the approach hurts. items.summary: This guide was originally published on the Hailbell blog. Short answer: If you get a few messages a week, a mailto link or a contact form is enough. For most apps, a hosted chat SDK (Intercom, Crisp, Zendesk, Hailbell) is the right call: an afternoon to install, and it handles the inbox, push for replies and storage for you. Build your own only if chat is the product itself. Whichever you pick, the work that decides whether it helps is the same: a button where people get stuck, a signed user identity, context with every message, push for replies, and deletion when the account goes. I build Hailbell, an in-app support chat for mobile apps, and use it in my own apps. The steps apply whichever SDK you pick. Swift examples use Hailbell's real API where it's named, and plain iOS code elsewhere. One section near the end covers where Hailbell fits, with its gaps, and the other SDKs. Building for Android too? The same decisions, in Kotlin, are in how to add support chat to an Android app. People don't go looking for support. items.title: US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off
items.summary: The privacy issues over the company’s surveillance cameras have caused protests in schools all over the country Angela Nguyen, a senior at Stanford University, has been on a mission to make sure her school doesn’t use automated license plate readers, like those made by Flock Safety, for mass surveillance. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people. Stanford cut ties with Flock this summer, and it’s not alone. The privacy reckoning over the company’s surveillance cameras is gaining momentum at schools nationwide. Since April, at least ten university campuses across seven states, have scrapped contracts with Flock. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

items.title: Why pharma firms are going to Earth's orbit in search of new cancer drugs (7 minute read)
items.summary: Varda Space Industries' autonomous factories carry miniature laboratories in which materials can be processed without astronauts. Once the process is complete, a capsule separates from the spacecraft and returns to Earth. The company currently has three spacecraft simultaneously in orbit. Manufacturing in space has several advantages, one of the most important being microgravity. Varda plans to launch seven missions in 2027 and 10 in 2028.

Users can adjust the speed of the GIF, edit individual frames, and share it. GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst are now available through the API.

items.title: Voice is Underutilized (6 minute read)
items.summary: Voice is a natural modality that is underutilized. It is great for rambling at coding agents and for capturing context. There is a lot of ambient context that exists in conversations with a ton of downstream value. This post presents some use cases for voice as a way to interact with AI.

items.title: Introducing Pangram Image 1.0 (5 minute read)
items.summary: Pangram Image 1.0 is an AI image and AI video detection model that can produce a heatmap localizing exactly where AI appears in images. It is robust to edits, compression, and low resolutions. There is a Chrome Extension available that can detect AI, as well as API support for images and video.

items.title: SpaceX's Starfall just went from secret to storefront (16 minute read)
items.summary: SpaceX has launched a commercial page for Starfall, a disk-shaped reentry capsule that can carry up to 1,000 kg of payload. The capsule can supply 1 kW of power and connect to the internet through Starlink, allowing researchers to pull data from experiments while in orbit instead of waiting for splashdown. It can be used for manufacturing, research, or testing and is aimed at biomedical customers, pharmaceutical companies, and materials science research. Starfall's timeline will depend on Starship - SpaceX is preparing for Flight 15, where it aims to catch both stages with the launch tower.

items.title: Ripple-65B Preview (4 minute read)
items.summary: Ripple-65B Preview is a frontier open-weight model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on TerminalBench 2.1. It surpasses significantly larger open-weight models from the US, including Reflection Beam 501B, Meta Muse Spark Open 816B, Thinking Machines Inkling 975B, and Nvidia Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B. The model was trained for only $32 million, one-tenth the estimated cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face, Together AI, GMI Cloud, and OpenRouter.

items.title: AI on the Ballot (18 minute read)
items.summary: Nearly every relevant local ballot measure opposing data centers won or is winning, with the exception of North Dakota. The constraint on AI dispersion is becoming political. AI will likely be a scarcity for much longer than expected. This post looks at what the implications might be if Americans don't change their minds about data centers.

items.title: How OpenAI Patched 948 Linux Vulnerabilities (12 minute read)
items.summary: OpenAI developed an autonomous pipeline for discovering, exploiting, and patching security vulnerabilities. In a single run, its cybersecurity model validated and generated patches for 948 Linux local privilege escalation vulnerabilities.

items.title: Apple Cuts Internal AI Usage Budgets in Move to Reduce Spending (5 minute read)
items.summary: Apple quietly lowered the daily spending cap on AI models for its employees last month. Some engineers had their budgets cut from $300 to $200, and the company is planning further cuts for some engineering teams that may potentially reduce their daily allowances to as little as $100. Groups outside of engineering may have their limits reduced to $25 from $100. Employees say that few workers were using their full $300 daily allowances, making the previous limits unnecessarily generous.

items.title: The Stacks Project, formalized in Lean (13 minute read)
items.summary: Axiom has released a Lean formalization of the entire Stacks Project. The Stacks project is an open-source reference that lays the foundation of modern algebraic geometry. The release is the largest integrated, reusable library of formalized mathematics ever built. It makes the full mathematical development of the Stacks Project available as a single, machine-checked library that researchers and AI agents can import from directly into new formal proofs.

items.title: Rebuilding the global town square from scratch (32 minute read)
items.summary: The new version of X.com's web app was built by five engineers working with AI coding agents in under six months. It loads pages significantly faster than the old web app over slow connections, and it already serves logged-out users and the pages that search engines crawl. This post covers why X.com was rebuilt, how the new web app is being rolled out, and how the old and new apps compare today. It also looks at the performance work completed since logged-out traffic moved over.

It can interact with both command-line interfaces and GUIs to perform a wide range of work and everyday tasks.

They are the perfect people to help figure out the shape of the future.
